title: NATO: what is it still for?
subtitle: 1949 to today
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Founded against the USSR in 1949, **NATO** should have disappeared with the Cold War. It is now bigger and busier than ever.

hero.hook: Built to face an enemy that has not existed since 1991, NATO has never had so many members.

blocks.text: **NATO**, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, is the most powerful military alliance in modern history. Founded in 1949, in the thick of the Cold War, it was meant to protect Western Europe against the expansion of the Soviet Union.

The disappearance of its enemy in 1991 did not dissolve it. The organization spent thirty years searching for a purpose, until Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended every doubt about what it was for.

sections.title: Origins: a shield against the Eastern bloc

blocks.text: NATO was officially born on April 4, 1949, when twelve countries signed the **[[North Atlantic Treaty]]** in Washington. The alliance answered an urgent need for security, with the Red Army occupying central Europe. Its first secretary general, Lord Ismay, summed up its mission in a line that stuck: “to keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.”
Iceland is the only NATO member with no standing army. Its contribution rests on radar stations, a coast guard, and hosting allied aircraft on its soil.

At the heart of the alliance sits **[[Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty]]**, which sets out collective defense: an attack on one member counts as an attack on all. Throughout the Cold War, this automatic solidarity deterred any Soviet offensive in Europe, since a direct war had become far too costly to risk.

sections.title: After the Cold War: enlargement and new missions

blocks.text: The fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the USSR in 1991 threw NATO into an identity crisis. With no designated enemy, the alliance looked obsolete. It chose instead to reinvent itself along two lines. The first was a massive enlargement eastward: former members of the **[[Warsaw Pact]]**, such as Poland and Hungary, then the Baltic states in 2004, joined the organization to guard against any return of Russian imperialism.

The second line was operational. NATO began acting outside its own territory, in the Kosovo war of 1999 and then in Afghanistan after 2001. The move eastward fed deep resentment in Moscow, where Vladimir Putin called it a provocation and a broken promise from the end of the Cold War.

sections.title: The shock of 2022 and the return of territorial defense

blocks.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, ended the age of doubt overnight. Within days, NATO rediscovered its founding mission: defending European territory. The shock pushed Sweden and Finland, neutral for decades, to apply for membership. Finland joined the alliance in 2023, Sweden in 2024.

blocks.caption: Since 2022, NATO countries have supplied Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and military training

blocks.text: The alliance, now 32 members strong, does not fight in Ukraine directly, so as to avoid **nuclear escalation**, but it coordinates logistical support on an unprecedented scale. The war has also forced a general rearmament in Europe, with Germany releasing massive funds to modernize an army neglected for thirty years.
The acronym of the organization exists in two mirrored forms, one for each official language: NATO in English and OTAN in French.

sections.title: NATO and the challenges of the 21st century

blocks.text: Beyond the classic Russian threat, NATO has to adapt to a new grammar of conflict. It has added **[[cyberspace]]** and outer space as official new domains of operation. Computer attacks on critical infrastructure now count as acts of aggression that can, in some cases, justify collective defense.

The organization is also looking toward Asia. China's rise has pushed NATO to build partnerships with Japan, South Korea and Australia, which worries some European members, who fear a drift away from the original geographic area.
NATO grew from 12 to 32 members between 1949 and 2024. It has repositioned itself as the central pillar of European security against Russia, while taking in new fields of conflict such as cyberspace.
